sources.name: Federal Reserve History: Asian Financial Crisis

steps.title: 1996: deficits in a boom
text: In 1996 Thailand imported **$74.9 billion** of goods but exported only $56.5 billion, a trade deficit of **$18.5 billion**. South Korea's deficit was $12.5 billion.
The map shows Thailand's trade balance with each partner: red where it bought more than it sold.

steps.title: July 1997: the baht falls
text: On **2 July 1997** Thailand devalued its currency against the US dollar, and the crisis spread across the region. International lenders, including the IMF, mobilized **$118 billion** of loans for Thailand, Indonesia and South Korea.
The map now shows how each economy's imports changed from the year before. Watch East Asia turn orange in 1998.

steps.title: Imports collapse
text: In 1998 imports fell by about a third: **−35%** in South Korea, −31% in Thailand, −34% in Indonesia and −26% in Malaysia.
Exports barely moved: Korea's fell 8% and Thailand's 5%.

steps.title: Deficits turn into surpluses
text: Because imports fell far more than exports, trade balances swung sharply. South Korea went from a **$12.5 billion** deficit in 1996 to a **$39.4 billion** surplus in 1998; Thailand from −$18.5 billion to +$11.7 billion.
Each line is one economy's balance with the world.

steps.title: The cost in output
text: Real GDP shrank by **13.1%** in Indonesia in 1998, 7.6% in Thailand, 7.4% in Malaysia and 4.9% in South Korea.
Measured in US dollars, Indonesia's GDP fell from $227 billion in 1996 to $95.5 billion in 1998. Korea rebounded fastest, growing 11.6% in 1999.
